title: So Hum
desc: The oldest mantra in the tradition is the sound the breath already makes. Nothing is added — you listen for what is there and let it hold your attention.

script.text: Sit so that the weight of your upper body drops straight down into the floor. Let the hands rest where they fall.
Do nothing to the breath. Let it be as short or as shallow as it wants to be for now.
Notice that the in-breath makes a faint sound at the back of the throat. Something like so.
And the out-breath makes a different one. Something like hum.
So on the way in. Hum on the way out. You are not saying it. You are noticing that it is already being said.
If the breath is too quiet to hear, imagine the sound instead. It works the same way.
So. Hum. Nothing else to do with it.
When you notice you have gone somewhere else — and you will — that noticing is not a failure. It is the practice. Come back to so.
So on the way in. Hum on the way out.
Let the mantra go. Sit with whatever is left.
Let the breath come back under its own management. Feel the floor again.

title: Counting the Exhale
desc: Counting only the out-breath, ten at a time. The narrowest possible task, which is why it works on a mind too busy for anything wider.
sourceTradition: Common to Yogic and Chan/Zen practice

script.text: Sit upright but not stiff. The spine long, the shoulders heavy.
Breathe in without counting. Then, as the breath leaves, count one.
In again, no count. Out — two.
Only the out-breath carries a number. The in-breath is free.
Go up to ten, then begin again at one.
If you find yourself at fifteen, the mind has gone for a walk. No matter. Start again at one.
If you lose the number entirely, start again at one. Beginning again is not starting over.
Keep counting. One to ten, then one again.
Now let the counting fall away and just breathe.
Notice whether the breath is different from when you began. It usually is.

title: The Pause Between Breaths
desc: Between the breath going out and the breath coming in there is a gap. The instruction is simply to be awake inside it. Nothing is held or forced.
sourceTradition: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra — the technique of attending to the turn of the breath
contraindications: Do not hold or lengthen the breath. If you have a respiratory condition, high blood pressure, or are pregnant, observe the pause without altering it.

script.text: Sit where you will not need to move for a while.
Let the breath find its own rhythm. This practice never asks you to change it.
Follow one breath all the way out. Notice that at the very end, before the next one starts, there is a pause.
It might be half a second. It does not matter how long it is. Only that you are awake inside it.
Rest your attention there. At the bottom of the breath, in the turn.
There is a second gap, at the top, after the in-breath completes. Find that one too.
Two still points in every breath. Nothing is being held. You are only noticing what was always there.
If the breath starts to feel effortful, you are interfering. Let it go entirely for three breaths, then return.
Stay with the turn of the breath.
Let the attention widen again. Feel the whole body breathing.

title: Cooling Attention
desc: For heat — in the body, in the temper, in the hour after an argument. Attention rests on the coolest sensations available and lets the rest follow.
sourceTradition: Ayurvedic sitali principle, adapted as attention rather than breath technique

script.text: Sit somewhere you are not too warm. Loosen anything tight at the neck or waist.
Take one slow breath in through the nose and notice something specific: the air is cooler going in than coming out.
Find that coolness at the rim of the nostrils. It is faint. Look for it anyway.
Every in-breath brings it back. Stay at the nostrils and let the coolness arrive again and again.
Now widen a little. Where else is the body cool? The palms, perhaps. The skin behind the ears.
Do not go looking for heat. Only for the cool places, and rest there.
If a hot thought arrives — something someone said, something unfinished — notice where it lands in the body, and then return to the coolest place you can find.
Cool air at the nostrils. Cool skin at the palms. Nothing to solve.
Let the whole face soften. The jaw, the space between the eyebrows.
Come back slowly. Heat does not leave in a hurry, and it does not need to.

title: Weight and Contact
desc: Attention on the places where the body meets the floor. The most reliable practice for a mind that will not settle, because weight cannot be argued with.
sourceTradition: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra — attention on the point of contact
contraindications: Attention on bodily sensation can be destabilising during a dissociative episode. If the body starts to feel unreal rather than heavy, open the eyes and name three things in the room instead.

script.text: Sit or lie down. Whichever lets you be heaviest.
Find where the body touches the floor. The sitting bones, the backs of the legs, the heels.
Do not describe it. Just feel it. The pressure, the temperature, the exact edge where you stop and the floor begins.
Now let weight go into those places. As if you were slightly heavier than you thought.
The floor is holding all of it. It has been the whole time.
Move to the hands. Wherever they rest, feel the contact — the weight of them, the warmth underneath.
Now the whole underside of the body at once. Every place that is being supported.
If the mind lifts off into planning, it will. Come back to weight. Weight is always here and it is never interesting, which is exactly what makes it useful.
Heavy, supported, still.
Before you move, notice the difference between the body you sat down with and this one.

title: Rotation of Awareness
desc: Attention moves through the body in a fixed order, resting a moment in each place. The order never changes, which is what makes it restful — there is nothing to decide.
sourceTradition: Yoga Nidra lineage; the 61-point rotation, shortened
contraindications: Sustained inward attention can be destabilising for people with PTSD or dissociative symptoms. Keep the eyes softly open, or stop, if it becomes uncomfortable.

script.text: Lie on your back, arms a little away from the sides, palms up.
We will move through the body in a fixed order. You do not have to remember it. Just follow.
Right hand thumb. Second finger. Third. Fourth. Fifth. The palm. The back of the hand. The wrist.
The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The shoulder. The armpit. The right side of the waist. The right hip.
The right thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle. The heel. The sole of the right foot. The right big toe.
Now the same on the left. Left hand thumb. Second finger. Third. Fourth. Fifth. The palm. The wrist.
The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The shoulder. The left side of the waist. The left hip.
The left thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle. The heel. The sole of the left foot. The left big toe.
Now the back of the body. The right shoulder blade. The left. The whole spine, from the base to the neck.
The back of the head. The crown. The forehead. The right eyebrow. The left. The space between them.
The right eyelid. The left. The right cheek. The left. The upper lip. The lower lip. The chin. The throat.
The chest. The stomach. The navel. The whole front of the body at once.
Now the whole body at once. Every part you just visited, all together.
Stay here. Nothing to do.
When you are ready, let one hand move. Then the other. Take your time coming back.

title: Silent Repetition
desc: A single word or syllable, repeated inwardly at the pace of the breath. The word matters less than the repetition, which is the whole method.
sourceTradition: Japa yoga; the three grades of repetition, of which the silent is the highest

script.text: Sit with the spine upright and the hands still.
Choose one word. Om, if nothing else comes. Or peace. Or a name that means something to you.
Say it once out loud, so the body knows the shape of it.
Now say it under the breath, barely moving the lips. Ten times, at whatever pace feels natural.
Now stop moving the lips altogether. Say it only inwardly.
Let it settle onto the breath. One repetition as the breath goes out, or one on each breath. Let it find its own place.
The word will change texture. It will get faster, or lose its meaning, or seem to say itself. All of that is fine.
When you lose it, pick it up again without comment.
Now let the word stop. Do not replace it with anything.
Sit in what is left of it.

title: The Sound and Its Ending
desc: Chanting Om aloud and then attending to the silence it leaves behind. Rousing rather than sedating, which makes it a morning practice.
sourceTradition: Mandukya Upanishad — the three sounds of Om and the fourth, the silence after

script.text: Sit upright. This one is loud, so choose your moment.
Take a full breath in, and on the way out let a long low sound come from the chest. Aaaa.
Again. Feel where it vibrates — low in the body, behind the breastbone.
Now the second sound, higher, in the throat and mouth. Ooooo.
And the third, with the lips closed, in the nose and the skull. Mmmmm.
Now all three, joined, on one breath. A into O into M.
Again. Let it be long. Let the M go on until the breath is gone.
Three more, at your own pace. Notice that the sound gets quieter each time without being told to.
Now stop. Do not chant. Listen to what the sound left behind.
That silence is the fourth part. It is the only part the text says is the real one.
Come back when the silence has thinned out.

title: The Fading Bell
desc: Follow one sound all the way down until you cannot say whether it is still there. The mind that follows a decay cannot also be arguing with anyone.
sourceTradition: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra — attending to a struck sound as it dies away

script.text: Sit still. If you have a bowl or a bell, have it within reach. If not, the recording will do.
Strike it once, softly.
Follow the sound. Not the strike — what comes after it.
It is getting quieter. Stay with it as it goes.
At some point you will not be able to say whether you are hearing it or remembering it. Stay there. That place is the practice.
When it is entirely gone, wait in the silence. Do not strike again yet.
Strike it again. Follow it down.
Again, if you like. Each time, the ear gets finer.
Now stop striking. Listen to the room instead — whatever is there. Follow the quietest thing you can find.
Let the listening go.

title: Watching Thought Arrive
desc: Not stopping thoughts, which cannot be done. Noticing that there is something present that is not the thought, and staying with that instead.
sourceTradition: Sankhya and Vedanta — the witness distinct from what it observes

script.text: Sit comfortably. This one asks for a little patience.
Do not try to have a quiet mind. Let it do what it does.
A thought will arrive. When it does, notice the arriving rather than the content.
Where did it come from? You did not decide to have it. It appeared.
Watch the next one appear the same way. Not what it says. That it came.
Now notice something else: whatever is doing the watching did not arrive. It was already here.
Rest as the thing that was already here. Let the thoughts pass in front of it like weather.
If you get pulled into a thought and forget — and you will — the moment you notice, you are back. There is no penalty.
Weather in front. Sky behind. Stay as the sky.
Let all of it go, including the image of the sky.

title: Wishing Well
desc: Four wishes, offered in a fixed order that always begins with yourself. The order is not sentimental — starting anywhere else tends not to work.
sourceTradition: Metta Sutta and the Visuddhimagga's fourfold order

script.text: Sit however you can be comfortable for ten minutes.
Bring to mind the phrase: may I be safe. Say it inwardly and see whether anything answers.
May I be well. May I be at ease. May I live with some kindness toward myself.
If that feels false, it often does at first. Say it anyway. It is a direction, not a claim.
Now bring to mind someone easy. Someone you are simply glad exists.
May you be safe. May you be well. May you be at ease.
Now someone neutral. Someone you see and do not think about — a neighbour, someone behind a counter.
May you be safe. May you be well. May you be at ease. They have a whole life you know nothing about.
Now, only if you are willing, someone difficult. Not the hardest person. Start further down the list.
May you be safe. May you be well. You are not excusing anything. You are declining to carry it.
Now let it go outward with no particular object. Whoever is nearby. Whoever is awake right now.
Come back to yourself, and end where you began. May I be well.

title: The Fire at the Navel
desc: Attention on the warmth below the navel — the classical seat of digestion. Warming and mildly rousing, so it belongs in the morning and not before sleep.
sourceTradition: Ayurvedic agni and the manipura chakra of the tantric body
contraindications: Not during acute heartburn, gastritis, ulcer, or in the first hours after a large meal. Not in pregnancy. If you run hot, use Cooling Attention instead.

script.text: Sit upright, with the belly free — nothing tight at the waist.
Rest one hand two fingers below the navel. Feel the warmth of the hand through the cloth.
Breathe normally and notice that the belly moves under your hand. Do not push it.
Now find the warmth underneath. Not the hand's warmth. The body's.
It is faint. It is always there. This is the fire the texts call agni, and everything you eat passes through it.
On each in-breath, imagine air reaching it. On each out-breath, imagine it glowing a little steadier.
Not bigger. Steadier. A fire that is too big digests the wrong things.
Stay with the warmth below the navel. Breath feeding it, quietly.
Now take the hand away and see whether you can still find the warmth without it.
Let it be. It will keep going without your attention, as it has all your life.

title: The Forest Floor
desc: Deep woodland, old ground, roots under everything. The heaviest of the five scenes, and the one to reach for when nothing will stay still.

script.text: Settle, and let the eyes close.
Put yourself on the floor of an old forest. Not a path through it — the floor itself.
Under you, a deep layer of leaves that has been building for longer than you have been alive.
Below that, roots. Not one tree's roots but every tree's, crossing and holding each other in the dark.
Nothing here is in a hurry. The tree above you has been at it for two hundred years and will be here after.
Smell the ground. Cold, mineral, faintly sweet.
Feel the weight of your own body pressing into the leaf litter, and the ground pressing evenly back.
Somewhere above, the canopy is moving. Down here it is entirely still.
Let yourself be one more heavy thing on the forest floor. Nothing is required of you.
The forest carries on. Let it. Come back slowly.

title: The Still Lake
desc: A lake at dusk, no wind. The classical image for a mind that has stopped being disturbed, and the coolest of the five scenes.

script.text: Let the eyes close and the shoulders drop.
A lake, late in the day. The light has gone flat and orange. There is no wind at all.
The surface is completely unbroken. It is holding the whole sky upside down without effort.
Notice that the water is not doing anything to be still. It has simply stopped being disturbed.
Something touches the surface — an insect, a leaf. Rings go out.
Watch them travel, get wider, get fainter. Watch the surface close over again.
This is the whole teaching. The lake does not mind being disturbed. It just returns.
Let a thought be a leaf landing. Rings out, rings fading, surface closing.
The light is going. The water is getting darker and even more still.
Leave the lake there. It will be like that all night.

title: The Hearth
desc: A fire in a grate on a cold evening. Warming and gently rousing, which makes it the scene for heaviness and cold rather than for agitation.

script.text: Sit, and let the eyes close.
A small fire in a grate. A cold room otherwise, and one warm side of you.
The heat is only on the front of the body. Your back is still cool. Feel both at once.
Watch what the fire actually does. It is never the same shape twice, and it never stops.
A log settles. A shower of sparks goes up and disappears.
There is no effort in it. Nothing is being achieved. It is simply burning because that is what it is.
Let the warmth on your face be the only thing you are attending to.
If you are tired or low, let the fire be doing the work for a while. You do not have to.
The fire is getting lower now, and steadier. Less flame, more heat.
Leave it burning down. Come back to the room.

title: Wind Through Grass
desc: An open hillside with wind moving across it. Light and clearing, for the days when everything feels thick and slow.

script.text: Sit upright. This one wants a little lift in the spine.
An open hillside, high up, nothing but long grass in every direction.
The wind is steady and not cold. It arrives in waves.
Watch a gust cross the field. You can see it coming before it reaches you — a line of movement travelling over the grass.
It arrives. It passes. Another one is already on its way.
Feel it on the skin. On the arms, the back of the neck, moving the hair.
Nothing here is heavy. Nothing here is stuck.
Let a breath in feel like the wind arriving, and a breath out like it passing on.
Waves of it, crossing and crossing. The field never stops moving and never goes anywhere.
Come down off the hill slowly.

title: The Night Sky
desc: Lying under an unlit sky. The most spacious of the five and the one that most reliably puts a problem back in proportion.
sourceTradition: Pancha mahabhuta — ether; the classical vastness meditations
contraindications: Vastness practices can be unsettling if you are prone to derealisation. Use The Forest Floor instead if this feels ungrounding.

script.text: Lie on your back if you can. Let the arms fall wherever they want.
You are outside, somewhere with no lights, on your back on the ground.
Above you the sky is completely open. No cloud, no moon. Just depth.
Let the eyes adjust in the way they do. More and more of it appears the longer you look.
Everything you can see is at a different distance. It only looks flat because we are so far from all of it.
You are lying on the outside of a planet, held on by nothing you can feel, looking out.
Whatever you were worrying about is still true. It is just a different size from up here.
Stay with the openness. There is nothing to reach and nowhere to get to.
Feel the ground at your back again — the one solid thing in all of it.
Come back in your own time.

title: Complete Rest
desc: Doing nothing, structured so the mind has something to follow. The practice most people skip and most people need.
sourceTradition: Hatha Yoga Pradipika — shavasana, with a modern tension-release order
contraindications: Late pregnancy: lie on the left side rather than flat on the back.

script.text: Lie down on your back. Feet apart, arms away from the body, palms up.
Take one breath in through the nose, and let the next one out through the mouth with a sound.
Two more like that. Each one, let a little more of your weight go into the floor.
Now let the breath go back to normal and stop managing it.
Squeeze the right fist tight. Tighter. Hold it. Now let it go completely.
Notice the difference between the two hands. That difference is what we are after everywhere else.
Squeeze the left fist. Hold. Release.
Now the shoulders — lift them toward the ears. Hold. Drop them.
Screw up the whole face. Hold it. Let it fall apart.
Press the backs of the legs into the floor. Hold. Release.
Now nothing. No part of the body has a job.
If a thought arrives, let it. You are not meditating. You are resting.
Let the body be as heavy as it wants to be.
Start with the fingers. Then the toes. Take a bigger breath. Come back without hurrying.

title: Yogic Sleep, Short Form
desc: The classical four-stage form — intention, rotation, breath count, return. Done lying down, at the edge of sleep without crossing into it.
sourceTradition: Yoga Nidra lineage — intention, rotation, breath count, return
contraindications: Sustained inward attention can be destabilising for people with PTSD or dissociative symptoms. Stop if it becomes uncomfortable rather than pushing through.

script.text: Lie on your back and get comfortable enough that you will not need to move.
The rule of this practice is one thing only: try to stay awake. Not alert. Awake.
Bring to mind one short intention. Something plainly true that you would like more of. Say it inwardly three times.
Now let it go. It has been planted and does not need attention.
Bring attention to the right hand. The thumb, each finger, the palm, the wrist, the arm, the shoulder.
The right side of the body, down to the right foot and the right big toe.
The left hand. The thumb, each finger, the palm, the wrist, the arm, the shoulder.
The left side of the body, down to the left foot and the left big toe.
The whole back. The whole front. The head and the face.
The whole body at once.
Now the breath. Count backwards from twenty-seven, one number per out-breath.
If you lose the count, begin again at twenty-seven. Losing it is expected.
Let the counting stop. Rest in whatever this is.
Bring the intention back once, in the same words.
Feel the floor, the room, the sounds outside. Move slowly when you move.

title: Three-Part Breath
desc: Filling the belly, then the ribs, then the upper chest, in that order. The foundation every other breath practice is built on.
sourceTradition: Classical dirgha; the complete yogic breath
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Keep it gentle in pregnancy — no forcing of the belly.

script.text: Sit upright with the belly free of anything tight.
Put one hand on the belly and one on the ribs.
Breathe in and let only the lower hand move. The belly rises. Nothing else.
Do that four or five times. Belly only.
Now add the ribs. Belly first, then the ribs widen sideways under the second hand.
Four or five of those. Belly, then ribs.
Now the third part. Belly, ribs, and last a little into the upper chest, under the collarbones.
Out in the same order, or simply let it all go at once. Whichever is smoother.
Ten breaths like this, at your own pace. It should never feel like effort.
Let it go entirely and breathe normally. Notice the difference.

title: Victorious Breath
desc: A soft narrowing at the throat that gives the breath an audible, oceanic sound. The sound is the point: it gives attention something to hold.
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Not with a sore throat or active respiratory infection.

script.text: Sit tall. The chin very slightly down, the throat soft.
Open the mouth and breathe out as if fogging a window. Feel where that happens — at the back of the throat.
Do it twice more. Learn the sensation.
Now close the mouth and make the same shape at the throat while breathing out through the nose.
There should be a quiet sound, like distant surf. Not a rasp, not a snore.
Now do it on the in-breath too. Both directions, same soft sound.
The sound tells you the pace. If it gets rough, you are working too hard.
Twenty breaths. Let the sound be the only thing you are listening to.
Release the throat and breathe normally. The sound stops. Listen to the silence it leaves.

title: Alternate Nostril Breath
desc: Breathing through one nostril at a time in a fixed cycle. The most balancing of the breath practices and the safest place to start with retention.
sourceTradition: Hatha Yoga Pradipika; the channel-purifying breath
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Skip if the nose is blocked — never force air through a congested side.
No retention in pregnancy or with high blood pressure.

script.text: Sit upright. Rest the left hand on the knee.
With the right hand, fold the index and middle fingers into the palm. The thumb and ring finger do the work.
Close the right nostril with the thumb. Breathe out through the left.
Breathe in through the left.
Close the left with the ring finger, release the thumb, and breathe out through the right.
Breathe in through the right. Close it. Out through the left. That is one round.
Keep going. In left, out right. In right, out left. Let the hand do it without your attention.
Aim for the two sides to feel the same. They will not, at first. That is what the practice is for.
Ten more rounds at your own pace.
Let the hand come down. Breathe through both nostrils and notice whether they feel more even.

title: Cooling Breath
desc: Breathing in over a curled tongue, which cools the air on the way past. The classical answer to heat, in the body and in the temper.
sourceTradition: Hatha Yoga Pradipika; the cooling breaths
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Not in cold weather or with a chest infection — it cools too effectively.
Skip if you cannot curl the tongue; use Hissing Breath instead.

script.text: Sit comfortably somewhere you are not cold.
Stick out the tongue and curl the edges up to make a tube. If it will not curl, use the hissing breath instead.
Breathe in slowly through that tube. The air will feel distinctly cool.
Draw the tongue in, close the mouth, and breathe out through the nose.
Again. In over the tongue, out through the nose.
Notice where the cool goes — the tongue, the throat, and then further down.
Twelve rounds, unhurried. If you start to feel chilled, stop.
Now close the mouth and breathe normally. See whether the coolness is still there.
Let it settle. Heat leaves slowly and does not need chasing.

title: Humming Bee Breath
desc: A long hum on every out-breath with the ears closed. The vibration fills the skull and leaves very little room for anything else.
sourceTradition: Hatha Yoga Pradipika; the bee breath
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Not with an ear infection. Do not press hard on the eyes if using that variant.

script.text: Sit upright somewhere you will not be overheard, or where you do not mind being.
Breathe in through the nose, ordinarily.
On the way out, hum. Mouth closed, a low steady sound, all the way to the end of the breath.
Again. Let the hum be lower than feels natural. Low vibrates more.
Now close the ears with the thumbs, fingers resting lightly on the head.
Hum again. With the ears closed the sound is suddenly inside the skull.
Stay with it. Feel where it vibrates — the face, the teeth, the crown.
Ten more, each one as long as the breath allows.
Take the hands down. Do not hum. Listen.
The quiet after bhramari is the reason for the noise.

title: Hissing Breath
desc: The cooling breath for people who cannot curl the tongue. Air drawn in through the teeth, which cools it the same way.
sourceTradition: Hatha Yoga Pradipika; the cooling breaths
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Skip with sensitive teeth or exposed roots — cold air on them is unpleasant.
Not in cold weather.

script.text: Sit comfortably. Let the jaw be loose.
Bring the top and bottom teeth lightly together and part the lips, as if grimacing.
Breathe in through the teeth. There will be a hissing sound and the air will feel cold.
Close the mouth and breathe out slowly through the nose.
Again. In through the teeth, out through the nose.
Ten rounds. Stop before you feel chilled — this cools faster than it seems.
Now close the mouth. Breathe normally.
Notice the difference in the mouth and throat.

title: Equal Breath
desc: In for four, out for four. The simplest ratio and the one to use when the breath is ragged and nothing else will settle it.
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.

script.text: Sit or stand. This one works anywhere and nobody can tell you are doing it.
Breathe in and count silently. One, two, three, four.
Breathe out for the same count. One, two, three, four.
If four is too long, use three. If it is too short, use five. Find the number that is comfortable and stay there.
The point is not the number. The point is that both halves are the same.
Ten rounds. Equal in, equal out.
If the count slips, that is information — the breath wanted to be a different length. Adjust and carry on.
Ten more.
Stop counting. Let the breath choose its own length again.

title: Extended Exhale
desc: Out for twice as long as in. The one breath practice with a direct, measurable calming effect, and the best thing to do at two in the morning.
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
If lengthening the out-breath makes you gasp on the next one in, the ratio is too steep. Shorten it.

script.text: Sit or lie down. This works lying in the dark, which is often when it is needed.
Breathe in for a count of four.
Breathe out for a count of six. Slower than feels natural, but not strained.
Again. In for four, out for six.
When six is easy, go to eight. In for four, out for eight.
Never force the in-breath to be short. Only let the out-breath be long.
Ten rounds. The out-breath is where the nervous system settles, which is why we spend longer there.
Keep going for as long as you like. If you fall asleep doing this, it has worked.
If you are coming back rather than sleeping, let the ratio even out first.

title: Bellows Breath
desc: Forceful breathing in and out through the nose at speed. Strongly heating and strongly rousing. The most contraindicated practice in the library.
contraindications: Do not practise in pregnancy.
Do not practise with high blood pressure, heart disease, epilepsy, glaucoma, hernia, ulcer, or during menstruation.
Not within two hours of eating.
Stop immediately at any dizziness.
Also avoid with detached retina. If you are new to it, do ten breaths, not thirty.

script.text: Read the cautions before starting this one. It is not for everyone and not for every day.
Sit upright, spine straight, hands on the knees.
Take two ordinary breaths first.
Now breathe in forcefully through the nose and out forcefully through the nose, at about one per second.
Both directions are active. The belly moves like a bellows.
Ten of those. Then stop and breathe normally.
Notice what happened. Heat, alertness, possibly a little light-headedness. If it is more than a little, stop here.
A second round of ten, if the first was comfortable.
Now stop entirely and let the breath find its own rhythm. Do not chase another round.
Sit still for a minute. The stillness after is as much the practice as the breathing.

title: Skull-Shining Breath
desc: Sharp exhalations from the belly with passive inhalations between. A cleansing practice rather than a breath practice, and classified that way in the texts.
sourceTradition: Gheranda Samhita; one of the six shatkarma
contraindications: Do not practise in pregnancy.
Do not practise with high blood pressure, heart disease, epilepsy, glaucoma, hernia, ulcer, or during menstruation.
Not within two hours of eating.
Stop immediately at any dizziness.
Stop at any pain in the abdomen.

script.text: Read the cautions. This one has real ones.
Sit upright with the belly free. Rest one hand below the navel.
The whole practice is this: a sharp pull inward of the belly, which pushes the air out through the nose.
The in-breath is not done. It happens by itself when the belly releases.
Try one. Sharp out. Let the in happen.
Now twenty, at about one per second. Only the out-breath is active.
Stop. Breathe normally and notice the effect.
A second round of twenty, if that was comfortable. Never push past comfortable.
Stop, and sit completely still. Do not go for a third round on the first day.
The clarity afterwards is what the texts are describing. Sit in it.

title: Breath of Fire
desc: Rapid even breathing through the nose, in and out at the same strength. Warming, and gentler than bhastrika, but still not a beginner's practice.
contraindications: Do not practise in pregnancy.
Do not practise with high blood pressure, heart disease, epilepsy, glaucoma, hernia, ulcer, or during menstruation.
Not within two hours of eating.
Stop immediately at any dizziness.

script.text: Sit upright. Read the cautions if you have not.
Unlike bhastrika, in and out are equal here — same speed, same strength, no emphasis on either.
Start slowly. In, out, in, out, through the nose, belly moving.
Now let it speed up until it is about two per second, still even.
Thirty seconds. If it becomes ragged, slow down rather than stopping.
Stop. Breathe normally. Feel the heat.
One more round of thirty seconds.
Stop and sit. Let the breath come all the way back to normal before you move.

title: Standing Deep Breathing
desc: Full breaths taken standing, with the arms. The practice to use when sitting still is not going to happen — first thing, or at a desk after too long.
contraindications: Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingling in the hands, or any tightness in the chest.
Lower the arms if you have a shoulder injury; the breath matters, not the reach.

script.text: Stand with the feet under the hips. Let the arms hang.
Breathe out completely first. Empty before you fill.
Now breathe in and let the arms float out and up, overhead.
Breathe out and let them come down the same way.
The arms are following the breath, not leading it. If they arrive first, slow them down.
Ten of those, unhurried.
Now the same breath without the arms. Just standing.
Feel the floor under both feet, and the breath moving the whole torso.
Stand still for a moment before you go back to what you were doing.

title: The Standing Stone
desc: A single upright stone in an empty field, weathered and unmoved. For the days when everything is in motion and nothing is holding.

script.text: Close the eyes and let the breath settle.
A field, open in every direction, and one standing stone in it.
Taller than you. Older than anything you can name.
Somebody put it there. Everyone who knew why is gone, and the stone is still standing.
Weather has been arriving at it for four thousand years. Rain, frost, sun, snow.
None of it moved the stone. It only changed the surface.
Put your hand flat on it. Cold, rough, absolutely solid.
Stand next to it for a while. Nothing is asked of you here.
The stone will be there tomorrow whether you come back or not.

title: What Is Under the Field
desc: The hidden half of a meadow — the roots, deeper than the grass is tall. For when the visible part of your life feels thin.

script.text: Let the eyes close.
A meadow at the end of summer. Grass to the knee, moving slightly.
Now go under it. Below the surface, into the dark.
The roots go down further than the grass goes up. Much further.
They are threaded through each other, holding the whole field together from underneath.
This is where the field survives the winter. Everything above it will die back and none of this will.
Stay down here where it is dark and cool and dense.
Whatever is visible about your life is the grass. This is the rest of it.
Come back up slowly, through the soil, into the light.

title: Rain on the Roof
desc: Inside, dry and warm, with rain coming down steadily outside. The most reliably comforting image in the set.

script.text: Lie down or sit back. Get properly comfortable.
You are inside. It is raining, and has been for a while.
Listen to it on the roof. Not a downpour. Steady, unhurried, going on all evening.
Every now and then the wind changes and it comes harder against one window.
Nothing out there needs you. Nothing is expected.
The rain will keep going whether you sleep or not.
Warm, dry, indoors, and the sound of water on the roof.
Let the listening go soft. Let the sound take over.

title: The Slow River
desc: A wide river moving too slowly to see, carrying everything downstream without effort. For letting go of something you have been holding.

script.text: Sit or lie down. Let the eyes close.
A wide river, deep and slow. So slow that from the bank it looks still.
It is not still. A leaf on the surface proves it — going, but taking its time.
Everything the river carries, it carries without any effort. It does not lift or push. It simply moves and things move with it.
Put something on the water. Something you have been carrying and are tired of.
You do not have to throw it. Just set it down on the surface and let go of the edge.
Watch it move away. Slowly. It may take a long time to be out of sight.
The river does not know what it is carrying and does not need to.
Come back to the bank when you are ready.

title: One Candle
desc: A single flame in a dark room, upright and unmoving. The classical concentration image, done with the eyes closed rather than open.

script.text: Sit upright, and let the eyes close.
One candle, in a room with no other light and no draught.
The flame is perfectly upright. Bright at the tip, blue at the base, still.
It does not flicker, because nothing is disturbing it.
Look at the darkest part, just above the wick. That is where the flame is not yet flame.
If the image slips or fades, that is expected. Bring it back. That bringing back is the practice.
One flame. Upright. Steady.
Now let the flame go out and stay with the after-image in the dark.

title: First Light on Snow
desc: Sunrise reaching a snowfield — cold ground, warm light. Rousing without heat, which makes it the morning scene for someone who runs hot.

script.text: Sit upright. The spine long, the head level.
A wide snowfield before dawn. Blue, silent, absolutely cold.
The light is coming but has not arrived. The sky is getting paler at one edge.
Then the first of the sun touches the top of the snow, and that edge turns gold.
Watch the line of light move down the field toward you. Slowly. It takes minutes.
The snow does not melt. It is still cold. But it is lit now, and that is a different thing.
The light reaches where you are standing.
Warmth on the face, cold underfoot, both entirely clear.

title: High Cloud
desc: Cloud moving fast across a sky, seen from below. For a mind that is already moving quickly and does not need slowing so much as widening.

script.text: Lie back if you can, or sit and tip the head slightly.
A bright day with high cloud moving fast. Not storm cloud. The thin high kind.
It is going somewhere at speed, and it is completely silent about it.
Down here nothing is moving. The speed is all up there.
Watch one piece of cloud cross the whole sky and go.
Another one is already coming. There is always another one.
Let your thoughts be the cloud. Fast, silent, passing, and none of them yours to hold.
The sky does not go anywhere. Only what crosses it.

title: The Open Window
desc: A window opened onto a spring morning, and the first air of the year coming in. For rooms and days that have gone stale.

script.text: Sit upright near where you imagine the window to be.
A room that has been closed all winter. You can smell that it has.
Now the window opens. The first air of the year comes in.
It is colder than the room and much cleaner. You can feel exactly where it reaches.
The curtain moves. Dust turns over in the light.
Breathe that air. It has come a long way and touched nothing on the way.
The room is changing while you sit in it. The staleness is going out the same window.
Leave it open.

title: The Empty Room
desc: A room with nothing in it. Not abandoned, not waiting — simply empty, and large. For when everything is too full.
contraindications: If emptiness reads as loneliness rather than spaciousness, use Rain on the Roof instead.

script.text: Sit, and let the eyes close.
A large room with nothing in it. Bare floor, tall windows, white walls.
No furniture. Nothing on the walls. Nothing to do in here.
It is not abandoned. It is clean and light and simply empty.
Notice that the room is not lacking anything. It is complete as it is.
Walk to the middle of it and stand there.
Your footsteps sound different in an empty room. Listen to that.
Nothing here needs arranging, deciding, or finishing.
Leave it empty when you go.

title: Before the Sound
desc: The silence a sound comes out of, rather than the one it leaves behind. The subtlest scene in the set and the one that repays repetition.

script.text: Sit upright somewhere genuinely quiet.
Listen to the room. Whatever is there — a fridge, traffic, your own ears.
Now listen underneath all of it, for whatever is left when you subtract each one.
There is something there that sounds arrive into. It is not silence exactly. It is more like room.
Every sound you have ever heard came out of that and went back into it.
Do not try to hear it. Just stop excluding it.
Stay there.
Let the ordinary sounds come back. They were never in the way.

title: Steady Gazing
desc: Looking at one point without blinking until the eyes water, then closing them and watching the after-image. Rousing, and the strongest concentration practice here.
contraindications: Not with glaucoma, recent eye surgery, or epilepsy — a flickering flame can be a trigger.
Use a steady object rather than a candle if you wear contact lenses.
Stop if the eyes hurt rather than simply water.

script.text: Set a candle, or any small steady object, at arm's length and level with the eyes.
Sit upright. The head does not move for the next few minutes.
Look at it. Not at the whole flame — at one point, the base of it.
Do not blink if you can help it. When the eyes water, that is the practice working, not failing.
Keep looking. Thirty seconds to a minute is plenty at first.
Now close the eyes. There will be an after-image.
Watch it. It will drift and change colour and slowly go.
When it is gone, open the eyes and look again.
Three rounds is enough. Concentration built this way is unusually stable.
Finish with the eyes closed. Let them rest.

title: Not This, Not This
desc: Setting aside everything you can observe, on the grounds that whatever is observing cannot be the thing observed. The most demanding practice here.
contraindications: Inquiry into the sense of self can be destabilising if you are already feeling unreal or detached. Use a grounding practice instead on those days.

script.text: Sit upright. This one is more like thinking than like resting.
Notice your hands. You can feel them, so they are something you are aware of.
Whatever is aware of your hands cannot be your hands. Set the hands aside. Not this.
Notice the breath. You can observe it. So it too is being observed. Not this.
Notice a sound. Observed, therefore not the observer. Not this.
Notice a thought. You saw it arrive. Not this either.
Notice a feeling, and the same is true of it. Not this.
Now look for the one doing the noticing. You will not find it as an object, because it is not one.
Rest in not finding. That is not a failure of the method. It is the method.
Come back gently. Pick the hands back up.

title: The Space in the Heart
desc: Attention resting in the middle of the chest, in the space the texts call the inner ether. Steadying without being heavy.

script.text: Sit or lie down. Rest one hand on the centre of the chest.
Feel the hand rise and fall. Do not change the breath to make it clearer.
Now find the space under the hand. Not the heartbeat — the room around it.
The texts say there is a space in there the size of a thumb, and that it contains everything.
You do not have to believe that. Just look for the space.
Breathe into it. Not literally — direct attention there on the in-breath and leave it there on the out.
If there is grief in the chest, it will show up here. Let it be in the space rather than pushing it out.
The space is bigger than what is in it. That is the whole point of the image.
Stay as long as you like.
Take the hand away and see if the space stays findable without it.

title: Listening to the Room
desc: No object, no mantra, no breath. Only whatever the ears are already doing. The easiest practice to do anywhere and the hardest to do for long.

script.text: Sit however you are. The eyes can be open or closed.
Do not do anything to the breath. Leave it entirely alone.
Listen. Not for anything. Just listen.
Notice the loudest thing first, whatever it is.
Now notice something quieter behind it. Something you were not attending to a moment ago.
And something quieter than that.
Stop hunting and let the ears do what they do without direction. Everything at once, nothing chosen.
Sound is arriving whether you attend to it or not. The practice is only to stop filtering.
If a sound annoys you, that is fine. Annoyance is also arriving. Let that be heard too.
Stay open for as long as it holds.

title: For Someone in Difficulty
desc: Turning toward suffering rather than away from it, with a wish rather than a plan. The practice for helplessness in the face of someone else's trouble.
sourceTradition: The second of the four brahmaviharas
contraindications: If you are in the middle of a crisis of your own, do Wishing Well first. Compassion practice draws on reserves you may not have today.

script.text: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle.
Start with yourself, and something in your own life that is genuinely hard.
Say inwardly: this is difficult, and I wish it were lighter.
Not fixing it. Only acknowledging it, which most of us skip.
Now bring to mind someone you know who is struggling.
May your pain be less. May you have some ease in it.
Notice the pull to solve it. Let that go. The wish is the practice; the solving is a different activity.
Widen it. Everyone awake right now for the same reason you sometimes are.
May it be lighter. For all of them.
Come back to your own breath. Let it be enough to have wished it.

title: Gladness at Another's Luck
desc: The least practised of the four and the most useful in an envious month. Being pleased about something good that happened to someone else.
sourceTradition: The third of the four brahmaviharas

script.text: Sit comfortably.
Bring to mind something good that happened to someone you love. Something recent.
Let yourself be pleased about it. Say inwardly: I am glad that happened to you.
Notice how easy that is when you love the person.
Now someone you barely know, who has had some luck. A colleague, an acquaintance.
May it continue. May there be more of it.
Now, if you can, someone whose good fortune you found difficult. Something that made you feel behind.
May it continue. Their having it does not take it from you — that is the belief this practice is aimed at.
Sit with whatever came up. Envy is not a moral failure, only a place attention gets stuck.
Finish with the first person again. The easy one.

title: What Is Not Mine to Carry
desc: The last of the four, and the one that keeps the other three from becoming exhausting. Caring without taking responsibility for the outcome.
sourceTradition: The fourth of the four brahmaviharas

script.text: Sit upright, and let the shoulders come down.
Bring to mind someone whose situation you have been carrying.
Notice where in the body you are holding it. Most people find the jaw, the shoulders, or the gut.
Say inwardly: I care about what happens to you, and it is not mine to decide.
Both halves are true. Dropping either one is how people burn out or go cold.
Again: I care about what happens to you. And it is not mine to decide.
Notice whether the holding place softened at all. It may not have yet.
Everyone is walking a road you did not build and cannot see the end of. Including you.
Rest there. Caring, and not carrying.
Come back and check the shoulders again.

title: Walking
desc: Ten paces one way, turn, ten paces back, at a quarter of normal speed. The practice for a body too restless to sit and a mind too busy to close its eyes.
sourceTradition: Chankramanam; cankama in the Pali sources
contraindications: Balance is reduced when walking this slowly. Use a wall or a rail if you need one.

script.text: Find a stretch of floor about ten paces long. Indoors is fine.
Stand at one end. Let the arms hang or clasp them behind you.
Look at the floor a few paces ahead. Not at your feet.
Now walk, at about a quarter of your normal speed.
Feel each foot: the heel arriving, the weight rolling forward, the toes leaving.
At the end, stop completely. Stand still for one breath before you turn.
Turn slowly and go back. The turn is part of it, not a gap between the parts.
Keep going. Ten paces, stop, turn, ten paces.
When the mind wanders — and it does, even walking — come back to the sole of whichever foot is on the floor.
Finish standing still at one end. Feel both feet at once.

title: The First Three Mouthfuls
desc: Three mouthfuls eaten with full attention at the start of a meal. Ayurveda treats how you eat as seriously as what you eat, and this is why.
sourceTradition: Caraka Samhita on the manner of eating; sadvritta
contraindications: If you have a history of disordered eating, close attention to food can be counterproductive. Speak to someone who knows your history before using this.

script.text: This one is done at the table, with food in front of you, before you start.
Put down the phone. Turn off whatever is playing. The texts are unusually firm about this.
Look at the food for a moment. Notice that you are about to eat, which most meals skip entirely.
Take the first mouthful. Do not chew yet.
Notice temperature first, then texture, then taste. In that order.
Which of the six tastes is here? Sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent. Usually more than one.
Now chew, and keep chewing past the point where you would normally swallow.
Second mouthful. Same attention. Notice the taste has already changed because the first one is still there.
Third mouthful. Then put the fork down for one breath before you carry on normally.
Three mouthfuls is enough. The rest of the meal will be different anyway.

title: Drawing the Senses In
desc: Deliberately taking attention back from each sense in turn. The hinge between the outward limbs of yoga and the inward ones.

script.text: Sit upright, eyes closed, somewhere reasonably quiet.
Start with sight, which is already handled — the eyes are closed. Notice what is left of it. Usually not nothing.
Now hearing. Do not block the sounds. Just stop going out to meet them.
Let sound arrive at the ear and stop there instead of travelling on into your attention.
Now smell. Whatever is in the room, let it be at the nose and no further.
Now taste. The mouth has a taste in it. Leave it in the mouth.
Now touch. The clothes, the seat, the air. All of it can stay at the skin.
Nothing has been shut out. You have only stopped sending attention outward to collect it.
Notice how much is left when the senses stop reporting. It is more than most people expect.
Come back out through the same doors, one at a time. Touch, taste, smell, hearing, sight.

title: Repetition on Beads
desc: One repetition per bead, once round the mala. The beads keep the count so the mind does not have to, which is more of a relief than it sounds.

script.text: Sit upright with a mala in the right hand, or any string of beads.
Hold it over the middle finger. The thumb moves the beads. The index finger stays off it.
Find the larger bead — the meru. You start next to it and you do not cross it.
Choose your word. Om, or a name, or a short phrase.
One repetition, one bead. Say it inwardly, then move the thumb.
The pace is whatever lets the word be complete. Not fast.
Keep going. The hand will find its own rhythm and stop needing you.
When you reach the meru, do not cross it. Turn the mala and come back the other way, or stop.
A hundred and eight is a long time and that is the point.
Put the mala down. Sit for a moment with the word still going without the beads.

title: Nothing Here Is Permanent
desc: A clear-eyed look at the fact that the body is on loan. Sobering rather than morbid, and it makes ordinary days noticeably better.
contraindications: Not during acute grief or when you are unwell. This contemplation needs a steady day to be useful rather than frightening.

script.text: Sit comfortably. This one asks for a steady day.
Feel the body. Warm, breathing, working.
None of the material in it was yours ten years ago. Almost all of it has been replaced.
It came out of food, which came out of soil and light, and it is going back.
This is not a sad fact. It is only a fact, and it is true of everyone who has ever lived.
Consider that the body will end. Not today. But it will, and you will not be consulted about when.
Now notice that it is working perfectly well at this moment.
Both things are true at once. That is the whole contemplation.
Ask what, given that, actually matters this week. Do not answer quickly.
Come back to the breath. Borrowed, working, here now.

title: Before the Day Starts
desc: Three minutes before anything else — before the phone, before the kettle. The classical daily routine puts intention first for a reason.
sourceTradition: Dinacharya; the sankalpa of the yogic morning routine

script.text: Sit on the edge of the bed if that is where you are. This works before you have properly woken up.
Do not look at the phone yet. Whatever is on it will still be there.
Notice the body first. How it slept. Whether it is heavy or light this morning.
That reading is useful — a heavy dull morning is kapha and wants movement; a wired restless one is vata and wants warmth and slowness.
Now one intention for the day. One. Short enough to remember at four in the afternoon.
Not a task. A quality. How you would like to meet whatever comes.
Say it inwardly three times.
Now let it go and stand up. It has been set.

title: The Six Tastes
desc: A short contemplation of what a balanced meal actually contains, done before eating. It changes what you reach for more reliably than a rule does.
contraindications: If you have a history of disordered eating, skip contemplations that focus on food.

script.text: Sit in front of the meal without starting it.
Ayurveda counts six tastes, not four food groups. Sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent.
A complete meal has all six, weighted toward the ones your constitution needs.
Look at what is in front of you and find them. Sweet is easy — grains, root vegetables, dairy.
Sour? Lemon, yoghurt, anything fermented. Salty is usually obvious.
Pungent — ginger, pepper, mustard, onion. Bitter — greens, turmeric. Astringent — lentils, beans, unripe fruit.
Which ones are missing? Most Western meals are short on bitter and astringent, which is why they sit heavily.
You do not have to fix it now. Just notice.
Eat. The noticing will change next week's shopping more than a rule would.

title: The Turn of the Season
desc: A contemplation for the fortnight either side of a seasonal change — the period classical texts single out as the most destabilising of the year.

script.text: Sit somewhere you can see or hear outside, if that is possible.
Bring to mind what season it actually is. Not the date — the weather.
Classical Ayurveda pays particular attention to the fortnight either side of a seasonal change.
That junction is when illness arrives, because the body is still running the last season's habits.
So: what is different outside now from a month ago? Light, temperature, damp, wind.
And what are you still doing that belonged to the last season? Eating cold food into autumn. Staying up as if it were still light at nine.
Pick one thing to change. Only one. The texts recommend changing gradually at a junction, not all at once.
Sit with the season as it actually is for a moment, rather than the one you had got used to.

title: Going Back Over the Day
desc: Retracing the day backwards, without judging any of it. Clears the mind before sleep better than trying not to think.
sourceTradition: Caraka Samhita's sadvritta, recalled at day's end
contraindications: If the review turns into self-criticism rather than recollection, stop and do Wishing Well instead. That is a different practice doing a different job.

script.text: Lie down or sit back. This is the last thing before sleep.
Start at now and work backwards. What happened in the last hour?
Do not evaluate it. Just recall it, the way you would recall a film.
Back further. The evening. The end of the afternoon.
If you find yourself arguing with something that happened, notice that and keep moving backwards.
The middle of the day. The meal. The morning.
All the way back to waking up.
Now notice one thing from the day you are glad about. It can be very small.
And let the whole day go. It is finished, whatever it was.
Nothing left to review. Sleep from here.

title: Oiling the Body
desc: Attention during the classical self-massage, which the texts prescribe daily and almost nobody does. Deeply pacifying for vata.
contraindications: Not over broken skin, an acute injury, or a fever. Not during acute indigestion.
Do not oil the body during the first days of menstruation, per classical guidance.

script.text: Warm the oil first — sesame for vata, coconut for pitta, mustard or none for kapha.
Start at the head if you are washing your hair, or at the feet if you are not.
Long strokes along the limbs. Circles at the joints. That is the whole technique.
Go slowly enough that you can feel the hand as well as the skin. Both ends of the touch.
The arms, one at a time. Shoulder to hand, circles at the elbow and the wrist.
The chest and belly, clockwise. Then the back as far as you reach.
The legs. Long strokes down, circles at knee and ankle.
The feet last, and give them longer than feels necessary. The texts are insistent about the feet.
Now sit or stand for a few minutes and let the oil stay on before you wash.
The word for oil and the word for love share a root in Sanskrit. That is not a coincidence.

title: Yogic Sleep, Full Form
desc: The complete form: intention, body rotation, breath, opposite sensations, brief imagery, and the intention again. The deepest rest in the library.
sourceTradition: Yoga Nidra lineage — the full form with sankalpa, rotation, opposites and visualisation
contraindications: Sustained inward attention can be destabilising for people with PTSD or dissociative symptoms. Keep the eyes softly open, or stop, if it becomes uncomfortable.
Not a substitute for sleep, and not to be done driving or operating anything.

script.text: Lie on your back. A pillow under the knees if the lower back asks for one. Get it right now, because you will not move again.
The only instruction is to stay awake. Not alert — awake.
Bring to mind a short intention. Present tense, positive, plainly true. Say it inwardly three times.
Now let it go completely.
Awareness to the right hand thumb, second finger, third, fourth, fifth. Palm. Back of the hand. Wrist. Elbow. Shoulder.
Right armpit, right waist, right hip, thigh, knee, calf, ankle, heel, sole, right big toe.
Left hand thumb, second finger, third, fourth, fifth. Palm. Back of the hand. Wrist. Elbow. Shoulder.
Left armpit, left waist, left hip, thigh, knee, calf, ankle, heel, sole, left big toe.
The back of the body. Right shoulder blade, left shoulder blade, the whole spine, the buttocks, the backs of both legs.
The front. The forehead, both eyebrows, the space between them, both eyelids, both cheeks, the lips, the chin, the throat, the chest, the navel.
The whole body at once. Every part you have just visited.
Now the breath. Count backwards from twenty-seven, one number for each breath out.
If you lose it, begin again at twenty-seven.
Let the counting go. Now feel heaviness — the whole body heavy, sinking.
And now lightness. The whole body light, floating, barely touching the floor.
Both at once, if you can. Heavy and light together.
Now an image, held loosely: a still lake at dusk, holding the whole sky.
Let the image go. Bring the intention back, in the same words as before.
Feel the floor. The room. Sounds outside. The breath moving on its own.
Move one finger. Then one toe. Come back in your own time, and slowly.

title: Falling Asleep
desc: Designed to be abandoned partway through. There is no ending, nothing to return from, and no chime.
sourceTradition: Modern synthesis of the yogic and clinical sleep-onset methods
contraindications: Do not listen while driving or doing anything else.

script.text: Lie however you sleep. This one is meant to be left unfinished.
You do not have to stay awake for this. If you go, you go.
Let the out-breath be a little longer than the in. Do not count. Just let it lean that way.
Now let the jaw be heavy. The tongue loose in the mouth.
The space between the eyebrows, soft.
The shoulders, further down than they were.
The hands, open.
The belly, doing its own breathing without any help.
The legs, heavy all the way to the feet.
Nothing left to hold. Nothing left to check.
The bed is doing all the work now.
Heavy. Warm. Nowhere to be.
Nothing more. Sleep from here.
